title: Entheogens: A Word and a Debate
description: How a 1979 coinage, a banker-mycologist and his critics shaped the study of sacred drugs

concepts.title: Naming the God Within
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1979 the Journal of Psychedelic Drugs printed a two-page proposal signed by the classicist Carl A. P. Ruck, Jeremy Bigwood, Danny Staples, Jonathan Ott and R. Gordon Wasson. They suggested a new word, entheogen, for plants and substances taken to produce religious experience. It's built from Greek entheos, "full of the god" or inspired, a word the Greeks used of prophets, poets and possessed worshippers, and -gen, "that which brings into being." Roughly, an entheogen is something that makes the god present within.

The authors wanted to replace two existing labels. "Hallucinogen" implied delusion and mental disorder. "Psychedelic," coined by the psychiatrist Humphry Osmond in the 1950s to mean "mind-manifesting," had become tied to the 1960s counterculture. A term built for ritual use, they argued, would let scholars describe a Mazatec mushroom vigil or a Vedic sacrifice without clinical or countercultural overtones.

Critics replied that the word is far from neutral. Call a substance god-generating and you seem to accept the participants' claim that a god is encountered, which a historian can't test. Others noted that the word is now applied loosely to any psychoactive plant in any setting, lumping together very different things such as a stimulant, a fermented drink and a vision-inducing brew. Many scholars still use it as a convenient label for ritual use. Some prefer plainer phrases such as "psychoactive sacrament," which name the substance and its role without endorsing a theology.

concepts.title: Wasson: Banker, Mushroom Hunter, Advocate
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert Gordon Wasson (1898 to 1986) was a vice president of the bank J.P. Morgan & Co. who turned an amateur passion into a research program. With his wife, the pediatrician Valentina Pavlovna Wasson, he argued in Mushrooms, Russia and History (1957) that whole cultures could be sorted into mushroom lovers and mushroom haters, and that such deep attitudes might preserve memories of ancient mushroom cults.

In 1955 Wasson took part in an all-night velada led by the Mazatec healer María Sabina in Huautla de Jiménez, Oaxaca, where psilocybin mushrooms were eaten. His article "Seeking the Magic Mushroom" in Life (May 1957) carried the ritual to millions of readers. Specimens he collected, grown by the French mycologist Roger Heim, let the Swiss chemist Albert Hofmann identify psilocybin and psilocin in 1958. Documents released decades later showed that the CIA's MKUltra program had helped fund a 1956 expedition, apparently without Wasson's knowledge.

The consequences for Huautla were heavy. Foreign seekers arrived through the 1960s, police suspected María Sabina of dealing drugs, and her house was burned. She later regretted showing the ritual to outsiders. Wasson went on to argue that the Vedic soma was a mushroom (1968) and, with Hofmann and Ruck in The Road to Eleusis (1978), that a sacred drink in Greek mystery rites contained ergot. His books were widely read, and they spread the claim that would define the field, that psychoactive plants may stand near the origins of religion itself.

concepts.title: Weighing the Evidence
concepts.contentHtml:
Each kind of evidence for drugs in ancient religion has its own weakness. If a hymn praises a sacred drink, you still can't tell from the words alone, since hymns are poetry and ecstatic language needn't mean a drug. Images are easily over-read. Wasson himself rejected the claim that a 13th-century fresco at Plaincourault in France shows a mushroom as the tree of Eden, accepting art historians' view that it is a conventional stylized tree. Plant remains prove presence, not use, since seeds can arrive as food, fiber or contamination. Ethnographic analogy borrows from living practice and risks assuming that distant peoples did the same.

Chemical residues are the strongest recent evidence. Wooden braziers from the Jirzankal cemetery in the Pamir Mountains of western China, about 2,500 years old, held burned stones with cannabis compounds pointing to plants unusually rich in THC (published 2019). On the smaller of two altars at the Judahite shrine of Arad in Israel, from the 8th century BCE, residue contained cannabis compounds, while the larger held frankincense (2020).

Two figures mark the extremes. Mircea Eliade's Shamanism (1951) dismissed intoxicants as a late, "decadent" substitute for true trance. John Allegro, a member of the Dead Sea Scrolls team, claimed in The Sacred Mushroom and the Cross (1970) that Christianity began as a mushroom cult, using speculative links between Greek, Hebrew and Sumerian words, and leading British scholars publicly disowned the book. Most historians now ask, case by case, whether independent kinds of evidence converge.

title: What Was Soma?
description: A lost Vedic plant and half a century of attempts to identify it

concepts.title: A Drink, a Plant and a God
concepts.contentHtml:
The Rigveda, composed roughly between 1500 and 1000 BCE, gives all 114 hymns of its ninth book to Soma, which is at once a plant, the juice pressed from it and a god. (The Roots of Religions topic covers its place in Vedic religion.) The hymns dwell on the ritual moment when the stalks are pressed and the juice is purified and poured for the gods. The poets praise its brilliance and tawny or ruddy color, and one hymn speaks of soma from Mujavat, apparently a mountain. Its effects are exhilarating: it inspires poets and emboldens Indra for battle. "We have drunk the soma; we have become immortal; we have gone to the light; we have found the gods," runs one verse (8.48.3).

The Iranian sister tradition calls the same substance haoma, and Zoroastrian priests still prepare it in the Yasna liturgy. The plant used for it in modern times, in Iran and among the Parsis of India, has been ephedra, a scrubby, almost leafless shrub. Brahmin priests who still perform soma rites in South India use other plants, such as the leafless climber Sarcostemma.

Already in late Vedic texts the original seems to have been hard to obtain: the Shatapatha Brahmana lists substitutes, such as putika, for when true soma cannot be found. The plant's identity was lost or obscured within the tradition itself. Since the 19th century scholars have proposed dozens of candidates, from fermented honey to cannabis, the opium poppy and the sacred lotus. Three proposals have dominated the modern debate.

concepts.title: Wasson's Fly Agaric
concepts.contentHtml:
In Soma: Divine Mushroom of Immortality (1968), R. Gordon Wasson argued that soma was the fly agaric, Amanita muscaria, the red-capped, white-spotted mushroom of northern birch and pine forests. It was the first serious proposal that soma was a fungus, and the book included an essay on the post-Vedic history of the soma plant by the young Sanskritist Wendy Doniger (then O'Flaherty).

His case had three main parts. First, the hymns never mention the plant's roots, leaves, flowers or seeds, which he read as fitting a mushroom. Second, the poets' color words and images of brilliance could, he argued, describe the mushroom's red cap. Third, he connected an obscure verse about men urinating soma to a practice recorded among some Siberian peoples, who drank the urine of a person who had eaten the fly agaric.

The leading critique came from the Cambridge Sanskritist John Brough in 1971. He argued that Vedic poetry is too figurative to support such botanical readings and that the fly agaric, whose effects often include nausea and drowsiness, fits poorly with a drink that roused warriors; a stimulant such as ephedrine fit better. Others noted that the mushroom grows with birch and conifers at high altitude, far from the plains of the Punjab, although the hymns do place soma in the mountains, and that its effects are notoriously unreliable. Wasson replied in print in 1972, and a few scholars kept his theory alive, but most Vedic specialists regard it as unproven.

concepts.title: Ephedra, Harmaline and the BMAC Evidence
concepts.contentHtml:
The strongest rival is ephedra, the plant Zoroastrians have actually used for haoma. Nineteenth-century observers recorded that Zoroastrians of Yazd in Iran used ephedra, locally called hum or homa, and sent it to the Parsis of India. In 1989 the Indologist Harry Falk argued that there was no need to look further. Ephedra contains ephedrine, a stimulant, and he read the texts as describing alertness, wakefulness and courage rather than visions. On this view soma was never a hallucinogen at all.

The same year David Flattery and the Iranist Martin Schwartz published Haoma and Harmaline, proposing Syrian rue (Peganum harmala), whose seeds contain the alkaloids harmine and harmaline. They made a strong case that rue served as a visionary drug in Zoroastrian Iran, but reviewers found the link back to the original haoma much weaker.

Archaeology entered the debate in the 1990s. The Russian archaeologist Viktor Sarianidi, excavating Gonur Depe and Togolok in Turkmenistan, sites of the Bronze Age Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex (BMAC, roughly 2300 to 1700 BCE), reported vessels in temple rooms holding traces of ephedra, poppy and cannabis, and called them rooms for preparing haoma. Later examinations, including one by the Leiden archaeobotanist Corrie Bakels (2003), could not confirm the identifications. Reviewing the debate that year, Jan Houben judged that ephedra remains a serious candidate. There is still no consensus, and some scholars doubt the question can ever be settled.

title: The Delphic Oracle
description: Plutarch's sweet-smelling vapor and a 21st-century geological theory

concepts.title: Plutarch's Pneuma
concepts.contentHtml:
For more than a thousand years Greeks consulted Apollo at Delphi through the Pythia, a woman who sat on a tripod in the innermost part of the temple, the adyton, and answered in the god's name. The most detailed ancient witness is Plutarch (c. 46 to after 119 CE), who served for many years as one of Delphi's two priests of Apollo. In his dialogue On the Obsolescence of Oracles, one speaker argues that prophecy happens when the Pythia's soul meets a pneuma, a breath or vapor rising from the earth, and that the oracle declined because this exhalation weakened. Plutarch adds that the room where consultants sat was filled, "not often nor regularly, but occasionally," with a fragrance like the costliest perfumes.

The same dialogue tells of a consultation held despite bad omens. The Pythia went down unwillingly, answered in a harsh voice "like a laboring ship," rushed toward the exit shrieking and collapsed; she died a few days later. Other writers supplied a physical setting. Strabo, writing around the turn of the era, reported that the oracle's seat was a deep cave with a narrow mouth from which rose a breath that inspired divine frenzy. Diodorus Siculus told how a goatherd named Koretas discovered the spot when his goats, and then he himself, behaved strangely near a cleft in the ground.

Plutarch's account sits inside a philosophical dialogue whose speakers weigh several causes for the oracle's decline, including the will of the gods and the depopulation of Greece. Still, it is the main ancient basis for the idea that something rising from the ground affected the Pythia.

concepts.title: Faults Beneath the Temple
concepts.contentHtml:
When the French School at Athens began its "Great Excavation" of Delphi in 1892, it found no chasm under the temple. In 1904 the British scholar Adolphe Paul Oppé argued that there had never been one, nor any vapor, and in 1950 the French archaeologist Pierre Amandry also rejected the vapors. Joseph Fontenrose's study of the recorded responses (1978) added that the Pythia seems to have spoken coherently, and that the frenzied priestess over a smoking crack was largely a later image. By the late 20th century most classicists treated the vapors as legend.

The Dutch-born geologist Jelle Zeilinga de Boer of Wesleyan University reopened the question. During a survey of active faults in Greece in the 1980s he noticed a fault running past the sanctuary. Working with the archaeologist John R. Hale, the geochemist Jeffrey Chanton and the toxicologist Henry Spiller, he argued that two faults, the east-west Delphi fault and the roughly north-south Kerna fault, intersect beneath the temple. Bituminous limestone below could release light hydrocarbon gases when the faults moved, and springs and mineral deposits mark where fluids once rose.

In a 2001 paper in the journal Geology, de Boer, Hale and Chanton reported methane, ethane and ethylene in water from the Kerna spring near the temple. Ethylene has a sweet smell and was used as an anesthetic in the early 20th century. Spiller compared Plutarch's account with clinical reports of light ethylene anesthesia, in which patients could remain conscious while feeling euphoric and detached. The team proposed that gas seeping into the adyton induced the Pythia's trance, and a 2003 article in Scientific American made the idea famous.

concepts.title: Doubts and What Remains
concepts.contentHtml:
Critics soon pressed on the numbers. The ethylene measured at Delphi was present only in tiny traces, far below anything known to affect people, and no one has shown that much higher concentrations ever existed there. In 2007 the historian of science Daryn Lehoux, in a paper with John Foster and in another of his own, argued that ethylene could not have produced the effects at plausible concentrations, and that fallback candidates such as benzene were "crucially underdetermined" by the evidence.

Geochemists also returned to the site. A team led by Luigi Piccardi (2008) found no hydrocarbon gas leaking at the surface today. They suggested instead that past earthquakes on the Delphi fault, which produced a magnitude 6.7 quake in 1870, could have briefly released carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulfide from deep pockets, and that memories of such episodes might lie behind the story of a vapor-breathing chasm. Others have proposed different agents altogether, such as burning or chewed oleander leaves, without direct evidence.

The faults are real and springs rise along them, which may help explain why the site drew a cult in the first place. That any gas shaped the Pythia's words is unproven, and many classicists think her state was a ritual trance shaped by training and expectation. A parallel argument, over whether the kykeon drunk at Eleusis contained ergot, is covered in the Mysteries & Hidden Faiths topic.

title: Peyote and the Native American Church
description: From a desert cactus to a Plains church and the Supreme Court

concepts.title: An Ancient Desert Sacrament
concepts.contentHtml:
Peyote (Lophophora williamsii) is a small, spineless cactus of the Chihuahuan Desert in northern Mexico and southern Texas. It contains mescaline and related alkaloids that alter perception and can produce visions. Its human use is ancient. In 2005 researchers radiocarbon-dated two peyote specimens from Shumla Cave No. 5, near the Rio Grande in Texas, to about 3780 to 3660 BCE and found that they still contained mescaline. The remains alone cannot show whether their owners used peyote in ritual, but they show the plant was gathered and kept about 5,700 years ago.

Written evidence begins with the Spanish. The Franciscan Bernardino de Sahagún, writing around 1560, described the Chichimec peoples of the northern deserts eating peyote to see visions and gain courage. Colonial churchmen saw idolatry: in 1620 the Inquisition in Mexico condemned peyote use as a superstition contrary to the Catholic faith. The practice survived. Among the Wixárika (Huichol) of western Mexico, peyote, hikuri, is a sacred being linked with the deer and with maize, and communities still make long pilgrimages to the desert of Wirikuta in San Luis Potosí, where they believe the sun was born.

The religion now practiced north of the border is younger. In the 19th century peoples of the Texas and Mexican borderlands, among them the Lipan Apache, Tonkawa and Carrizo, are thought to have shaped an all-night peyote ceremony and passed it north. By the 1880s it had reached the Kiowa and Comanche, newly confined to reservations in Indian Territory, later Oklahoma.

concepts.title: Quanah Parker and the Peyote Road
concepts.contentHtml:
The peyote religion spread across the Plains in the last decades of the 19th century, a time of catastrophe. The bison herds had been destroyed, the Red River War of 1874 to 1875 ended free Comanche and Kiowa life, and the Ghost Dance, another response to crisis, was crushed after Wounded Knee in 1890. Peyote meetings offered healing, prayer and a moral code, the "peyote road."

Its most famous early champion was Quanah Parker (c. 1845 to 1911), son of the Comanche leader Peta Nocona and Cynthia Ann Parker, a captured settler girl raised as a Comanche. Quanah helped lead the last Quahada band onto the reservation near Fort Sill in 1875, then became a rancher, a judge and the government's chosen principal chief. He also led peyote meetings and defended them before officials. A story told in several versions says he first took peyote when a Mexican healer treated his fever after a bull gored him in Texas; it is tradition, not documented fact. So is the saying credited to him: "The white man goes into his church and talks about Jesus; the Indian goes into his tipi and talks to Jesus."

A meeting runs all night in a tipi around a fire and a crescent-shaped earthen altar, with prayer, songs to a water drum and gourd rattle, and peyote taken as sacrament and medicine. A road man leads, helped by a drum chief, a cedar man and a fire man. The Half Moon way is associated with the Kiowa and Comanche; the Cross Fire, descended from the Big Moon rite of the Caddo-Delaware leader John Wilson, uses the Bible more openly.

concepts.title: Peyote in Court
concepts.contentHtml:
Missionaries and Indian agents campaigned against peyote for decades, and many states banned it. In 1918, while Congress considered a federal ban, the Smithsonian ethnologist James Mooney, who had attended meetings, testified in the peyotists' defense and then helped Oklahoma members incorporate as the Native American Church. Courts slowly accepted the religion. In People v. Woody (1964) California's Supreme Court overturned the convictions of Navajo members, and when federal law later controlled peyote, a regulation exempted the Church's sacramental use.

The crisis came with Employment Division v. Smith (1990). Alfred Smith, a Klamath man, and his colleague Galen Black lost their jobs at an Oregon drug-rehabilitation program after taking peyote at a Native American Church ceremony, and the state denied them unemployment benefits for "misconduct." Oregon's drug law had no religious exemption. Writing for the Supreme Court, Justice Antonin Scalia held that a neutral, generally applicable law does not violate the free exercise of religion even if it burdens a religious practice, so the state need not show a "compelling interest." Justice Sandra Day O'Connor agreed with the result but not the reasoning, and three justices dissented.

Religious groups of every kind were alarmed. Congress passed the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA, 1993), without dissent in the House and 97 to 3 in the Senate, restoring the compelling-interest test; in City of Boerne v. Flores (1997) the Court held that it could not be applied to the states. A campaign led by Native leaders such as Reuben Snake (Ho-Chunk) then won the 1994 amendments to the American Indian Religious Freedom Act, making ceremonial peyote use by members of federally recognized tribes lawful in every state.

title: Ayahuasca Churches
description: Santo Daime, the União do Vegetal and a sacrament that crossed borders

concepts.title: The Vine of the Souls
concepts.contentHtml:
Ayahuasca is a Quechua name often translated "vine of the souls" or "vine of the dead," from aya (spirit, corpse) and waska (rope, vine). It names a brew made chiefly from the Amazonian vine Banisteriopsis caapi, usually combined with the leaves of another plant that contain DMT. Pharmacologists explain why the pairing matters: DMT swallowed alone is broken down in the gut, but harmala alkaloids in the vine block the enzyme responsible, monoamine oxidase. The result is hours of intense visions, often with vomiting, which many users regard as purification. The same enzyme-blocking action makes the brew dangerous in combination with some medicines, notably many antidepressants.

Many Indigenous peoples of the western Amazon use it under names such as yagé and caapi, for healing, divination and dealings with spirits, and in the Peruvian Amazon mestizo healers called vegetalistas built their own tradition around it. How old the brew is remains debated. No ancient residue of it has been found, and some anthropologists argue that its wide spread across the region happened within the last few centuries, shaped by missions and the rubber economy.

A related find shows that the chemistry was known long before. A ritual bundle from the Cueva del Chileno in highland Bolivia, about 1,000 years old, held a pouch bearing traces of harmine and DMT along with compounds from coca, reported in 2019. How they were taken is unknown, and snuff is as likely as a drink. In the 20th century the regional practice gave rise to something new: churches with hymns, doctrine and membership, founded on Brazil's rubber frontier.

concepts.title: Santo Daime and the União do Vegetal
concepts.contentHtml:
Santo Daime began with Raimundo Irineu Serra (1892 to 1971), a Black Brazilian from Maranhão who migrated to the Amazon in 1912 during the rubber boom. After drinking ayahuasca in Acre, near the borders with Bolivia and Peru, he had visions of a woman he came to identify as the Virgin of Conception, the Queen of the Forest, who gave him a mission. From about 1930 he led ceremonies near Rio Branco. Members call the drink Daime, linked to the prayer "dai-me" ("give me"), as in "give me strength, give me love." Services, called works, feature hymns received by the founder and later members, participants in uniform dancing in ordered rows, and a double-barred cross. The doctrine blends folk Catholicism, Spiritism and Afro-Brazilian and Indigenous elements. After Irineu's death the movement split. The branch led by Sebastião Mota de Melo, now called ICEFLU, founded the forest community of Céu do Mapiá and carried the church abroad.

The União do Vegetal (UDV) was founded in 1961 by José Gabriel da Costa, known as Mestre Gabriel (1922 to 1971), a rubber tapper from Bahia working in the western Amazon. Members call the tea hoasca or simply the Vegetal and drink it in sessions devoted to "mental concentration," with teaching given through chanted "calls" and through questions and answers. The UDV is more restrained in style than Santo Daime: members stay seated, a hierarchy of trained mestres leads, and its Christian and Spiritist doctrine includes reincarnation. Its headquarters is now in Brasília, and it has branches abroad, including in the United States.

concepts.title: Law, Courts and Tourists
concepts.contentHtml:
Brazil put the ayahuasca vine on its list of banned substances in 1985, then lifted the ban after a federal drug council studied the churches. In 2010 the National Council on Drug Policy (CONAD) issued rules that permit religious use but prohibit selling the brew or profiting from it, using it outside religious rituals, promoting it to tourists and offering it as therapy without scientific support.

Abroad, the churches went to court. In 1999 US Customs agents seized more than 30 gallons of hoasca shipped from Brazil to the UDV branch in Santa Fe, New Mexico, led by Jeffrey Bronfman. The church sued under RFRA, and in Gonzales v. O Centro Espírita Beneficente União do Vegetal (2006) the Supreme Court ruled 8 to 0, in an opinion by Chief Justice John Roberts, that the government had not shown a compelling interest in barring the church's use. The long-standing peyote exemption, the Court noted, undercut the claim that drug law can admit no exceptions. A federal court protected a Santo Daime church in Oregon in 2009. DMT is controlled under the 1971 UN Convention on Psychotropic Substances, but the International Narcotics Control Board has said that plant brews such as ayahuasca are not.

Meanwhile ayahuasca tourism grew, centered on Iquitos in Peru, from the 2000s. In 2008 Peru declared the traditional use of ayahuasca by Amazonian Indigenous communities part of the national cultural heritage. Critics point to participants' deaths, sexual abuse by some facilitators, drug interactions, pressure on wild vines and the commodification of Indigenous knowledge. In April 2018 the Shipibo-Konibo healer Olivia Arévalo, aged about 81, was shot dead in Ucayali, and a Canadian visitor whom local residents blamed was lynched.

title: Ritual, Cannabis, Alcohol and Tobacco
description: Rastafari's herb, sacred tobacco, sacramental wine and what the comparison shows

concepts.title: The Holy Herb of Rastafari
concepts.contentHtml:
Rastafari arose in Jamaica in the 1930s, after Ras Tafari Makonnen was crowned Emperor Haile Selassie I of Ethiopia in 1930 and preachers such as Leonard Howell proclaimed him the messiah. (The Mix-and-Match Faiths topic covers its wider history.) For many Rastafari, cannabis, called ganja, "the herb" or "the holy herb," is a sacrament. It clears the mind for "reasoning," the communal discussion of scripture and life, and helps the smoker find the divinity within. It is shared in a chalice or pipe, often after a prayer, at small groundings and at large Nyabinghi gatherings with drumming and chanting. Members cite verses such as Psalm 104:14, which in the King James Version reads "He causeth the grass to grow for the cattle, and herb for the service of man," and Revelation 22:2, "the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations."

The word ganja comes from Hindi, and Jamaican use of the plant probably owes something to the Indian indentured laborers who arrived from 1845, as well as to Afro-Jamaican traditions such as Kumina and to widespread popular use. Howell's commune at Pinnacle, founded in 1940, grew ganja and was raided by police again and again. Not all Rastafari use the herb; some abstain.

The law has moved unevenly. South Africa's Constitutional Court refused a religious exemption in the Prince case (2002) by 5 votes to 4, though in 2018 it decriminalized private adult use on privacy grounds. Jamaica's Dangerous Drugs (Amendment) Act of 2015 decriminalized small amounts and allowed sacramental use by Rastafari, and Barbados passed a sacramental cannabis law in 2019.

concepts.title: Sacred Tobacco
concepts.contentHtml:
Tobacco is an American plant. Indigenous peoples cultivated several species, including Nicotiana rustica, far stronger in nicotine than the commercial N. tabacum. Its use is very old: charred wild tobacco seeds in a hearth at the Wishbone site in Utah's Great Salt Lake Desert, reported in 2021, date to about 12,300 years ago, the oldest evidence of human use. The seeds alone cannot show whether that use was ritual.

In many Native traditions tobacco is less a habit than a means of prayer. Smoke is understood to carry words to the Creator and the spirits, and loose tobacco is offered when asking an elder for teaching, before gathering a medicine plant or at a grave. Among the Anishinaabe it is asemaa, first of the sacred medicines. The Lakota sacred pipe, the chanunpa, is traced in tradition to White Buffalo Calf Woman, and smoking it seals prayers and binding promises. In 1673 the French Jesuit Jacques Marquette described the calumet, a ceremonial pipe whose presentation brought peace and safe passage among the Illinois and their neighbors. Haudenosaunee ceremonies burn tobacco to send thanks upward. In South America, as the anthropologist Johannes Wilbert documented in Tobacco and Shamanism in South America (1987), many shamans treat tobacco as a powerful spirit and teacher.

This sacred use sits beside a public-health crisis. American Indian and Alaska Native adults have the highest rates of commercial cigarette smoking of any group in the United States. Many tribal health programs now teach a distinction between "traditional" or "sacred" tobacco, used sparingly and with ceremony, and commercial tobacco, an addictive product sold for profit.

concepts.title: Wine at the Altar, and the Comparison
concepts.contentHtml:
Wine has a fixed place in Jewish and Christian ritual. Jewish households sanctify the Sabbath and festivals with a blessing over a cup of wine, the kiddush, and the Mishnah requires even the poorest Jew to drink four cups at the Passover Seder. In Christianity wine is one of the two elements of the Eucharist, recalling the Last Supper, and Catholic canon law requires it to be "natural, made from grapes of the vine, and not corrupt." The temperance movement pushed many Protestants toward grape juice: in 1869 the Methodist dentist Thomas Bramwell Welch of Vineland, New Jersey, pasteurized "Dr. Welch's Unfermented Wine" for communion. When the United States banned alcohol, the Volstead Act (1919) still allowed wine for sacramental purposes, an exemption some bootleggers abused by posing as clergy. Islam forbids wine, yet Sufi poets made it a metaphor for divine love.

"Drug" and "sacrament" are social categories. The country that let priests and rabbis obtain wine during Prohibition let many states prosecute peyote users. Peyote and ayahuasca won legal protection through long-established communities, sincere belief and religious freedom law; cannabis, with its huge recreational market, has seldom won religious exemptions outside Jamaica and Barbados.

In every case ritual sets rules about who takes the substance, when, with whom and for what end. The psychiatrist Norman Zinberg's Drug, Set, and Setting (1984) argued that the effects of a drug depend on the user's expectations and surroundings as much as on chemistry.
